bio.en: Ami Vora is Chief Product Officer at Faire, the leading B2B marketplace for independent retailers and brands, and was employee #150 at Facebook, where she launched the first developer platform and led global ads and WhatsApp product/design.
bio.zh: Ami Vora 是 Faire（面向独立零售商与品牌的最大 B2B 市场）首席产品官，也是 Facebook 第 150 号员工，曾发布首个开发者平台，并领导全球广告业务及 WhatsApp 的产品与设计。

summary.en: Ami discusses the skill of disagreeing skillfully—subordinating your ego to get to the best outcome—and using metaphors and imagery to rally a team around a shared feeling. She introduces the “hill climb” metaphor to distinguish local from global optima and what sustains you through the valley. The conversation covers building strategy skills, being a successful woman in tech, and setting up effective goals, plus a fun lightning round.
summary.zh: Ami 探讨了“优雅地异议”这门艺术——把自我收起来，只为达成最好的结果——以及用隐喻和意象让团队围绕共同感受团结一致。她提出“爬山”隐喻来区分局部最优与全局最优，以及是什么支撑你穿越低谷。对话涵盖策略能力、身为科技行业女性的成功之道、设定有效目标，以及一轮有趣的快问快答。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Boz, the CTO of Meta, said something about you. "Working with Ami, she could have the most profound disagreement in the world and she would respond, fascinating, you have to tell me more why you think that."
turns.zh: Meta CTO Boz 说过你一些事。「和 Ami 工作，她可以和人有世界上最深的分歧，她会回应：有趣，你得告诉我更多你为什么那么想。」

turns.speaker: Ami Vora
turns.en: I really enjoy being right and then it turns out in the working world, that did not serve me so great. I think the hard part is sublimating your ego a little bit and saying it's more important to get to the outcome than to be right.
turns.zh: 我很享受being right，然后 turns out 在工作世界里，那对我没那么好用。难的是 sublimating 你的 ego 一点，说到达结果比 being right 更重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this very tactical piece of advice when you're trying to come up with a metaphor or analogy, think about what you want your users to feel when you're using the product.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个非常战术的建议：当你试图想出 metaphor 或 analogy，想你用户用产品时你希望他们感受什么。

turns.speaker: Ami Vora
turns.en: If we all agree that the feeling of something should be, I'm sitting in Dolores Park with my friends on a sunny Saturday, then people will just naturally build something that feels more consistent.
turns.zh: 如果我们都同意某个东西的感觉应该是「一个阳光的周六我和朋友坐在 Dolores Park」，大家就会自然 build 出感觉更一致的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's also this metaphor about the hill climb.
turns.zh: 还有这个爬山 metaphor。

turns.speaker: Ami Vora
turns.en: For me, the hill climb is all about the difference between a local optimum and a global optimum. You're standing on top of the hill, you're looking down, you can see rolling hills, the sheep, the grass, whatever, but then, way off in the distance you can see a mountain. And the thing that gets me through the valley is remembering what the summit feels like.
turns.zh: 对我来说爬山全是关于 local optimum 和 global optimum 的区别。你站在山顶往下看，能看到 rolling hills、羊、草什么的，但远处你能看到一座山。带我穿过山谷的是记得 summit 感觉像什么。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Today, my guest is Ami Vora. Ami is Chief Product Officer at Faire, which connects independent retailers and brands around the world, and I believe is the most successful and biggest B2B marketplace startup out there. Prior to Faire, Ami was employee 150 at Facebook, where she launched the first Facebook developer platform and was later head of product for the $55 billion global Facebook ads business. She also oversaw the introduction of ads on the Instagram platform and most recently, she led product and design for the largest messaging app in the world, WhatsApp. (00:01:34): In our conversation we cover a lot of ground, including building your strategy skills, how to disagree with people skillfully, being a successful woman in tech, using metaphors and imagery to rally your team and get your point across, setting up effective goals, plus a bunch of jokes in the lightning round that you don't want to miss. This was a really special and authentic conversation that I'm very excited to bring to you. With that, I bring you, Ami Vora. (00:02:03): Ami, thank you so much for being here and welcome to the podcast.
turns.zh: 今天的嘉宾是 Ami Vora。Ami 是 Faire 的首席产品官，Faire 连接全球独立零售商和品牌，我相信是最成功最大的 B2B 市场创业公司。在 Faire 之前，Ami 是 Facebook 第 150 号员工，发布了第一个 Facebook 开发者平台，后来领导 550 亿美元全球 Facebook 广告业务的产品。她也监督了 Instagram 平台广告的引入，最近领导了世界最大消息 app WhatsApp 的产品和设计。(00:01:34)：在我们对话里我们覆盖很多，包括建战略技能、怎么 skillfully 不同意、在科技界做成功女性、用 metaphor 和意象 rally 团队和传达观点、设有效目标，加上闪电问答里一堆笑话你别错过。这是一次非常特别和真实的对话，我很兴奋带给你。下面请出 Ami Vora。(00:02:03)：Ami，非常感谢你来，欢迎来到播客。

turns.speaker: Ami Vora
turns.en: Oh, thank you. I'm so happy to be here.
turns.zh: 哦，谢谢。我超开心来这里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, when I asked you about your goal for our conversation today, you said the most amazing thing, which I love. You said that your goal is to be as authentic as possible and to show that people can be pretty messy and imperfect at times, yet still be very successful. I love that so much. Let's definitely try to do this. Is there anything else you want to add on that?
turns.zh: 当我问你今天对话的目标时，你说了最 amazing 的事，我很爱。你说你的目标是尽可能真实，展示人有时可以挺乱、不完美，但仍可非常成功。我超爱那个。让我们一定要做这个。还有什么想加的？

turns.speaker: Ami Vora
turns.en: Yeah, I mean, maybe I'll just say a couple more words on that. Actually, I feel like when I was coming up, when I looked at people who were successful, they seemed to have everything figured out, especially the women. They were all super women, where they respond to every email in 10 seconds, they didn't seem to sleep, they always wore high heels. They were just perfect and I was just like, oh, I guess I'm never going to be successful. That is not me. I love to sleep, I waste time doing absurd things all the time. (00:03:00): And I'll tell you how glamorous my lifestyle is, I'm currently working out of my bathroom. I'm talking to you from my bathroom, which is where I work from because I love my house, it's a great house, wasn't meant for work from home, three kids, two parents remote work, and it was just the place with the most closing doors between me and my children when the pandemic started. And so it just took me a while to realize that actually, it's all fine. No one's got it fully figured out, you never know how someone else is living. Most of us are winging it and learning as we're going and learning through trial and error and it's all normal. It's all fine and I can do it and you can do it, and everyone.
turns.zh: 对，也许我就多说几句。其实我觉得我成长时，看成功的人他们好像什么都想通了，尤其女性。她们都是超级女性，10 秒回每封邮件、似乎不睡觉、总穿高跟鞋。她们就是完美，我就想哦我永远成功不了。那不是我。我爱睡觉、我浪费时间做荒谬的事。(00:03:00)：告诉你我的生活方式多 glamorous，我现在在浴室工作。我从浴室和你说话，这是我工作的地方因为我爱我的房子、是好房子，但不是为远程工作设计的，三个孩子、两个家长远程工作，它是疫情开始时我和孩子之间最多关着的门的地方。所以我花了一阵 realize 其实都 fine。没人全想通了，你从不知道别人怎么活。我们大多在 winging it、边走边学、trial and error，都正常。都 fine，我能做、你能做、每个人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I so love hearing this. This is something people often want to hear more of on this podcast, because there's all these stories of here's all these successes, here's all these things I did and everything, it just always seems to work out. And we try to, we have this failure corner on the podcast where people share story failure. So I love just setting that frame for this conversation of just super being real and being clear that there's a lot of things that go wrong behind the scenes that people often don't hear about.
turns.zh: 我超爱听这个。这是这播客上大家常想多听的，因为有所有这些成功故事、所有这些我做的事、一切，似乎总顺。我们尝试有 failure corner 大家分享失败故事。所以我爱为这次对话设这个框架——超级真实、清楚幕后有很多出问题的事大家常没听到。

turns.speaker: Ami Vora
turns.en: I for a long time felt like I was held back because I don't have a plan, but I realized that probably the most important thing is to just acknowledge that that is true for me. That I'm not going to be a person with a plan, and actually the thing that has consistently served me is to do the thing that feels right, go to the place that feels like home, work with the people who feel like my friends. Just work where when I put on the code of the job, I feel like, oh, this is a place where I could really be lucky, I could be creative, I'm in the right spot, as opposed to feeling like, oh, there is an end state that I know of and I'm just going to have to work my way to that end state. Whenever I get in that zone of, there's only one outcome and I just have to get there, I'm not my best. I'm not bringing the creativity and the luck and the excitement in the same way.
turns.zh: 我很长时间觉得我被 held back 因为我没有计划，但我 realize 大概最重要的是承认那对我是真的。我不会是有计划的人，其实一直 serve 我的是做感觉对的事、去感觉像家的地方、和感觉像朋友的人 work。就穿上那份工作的外衣时我感觉哦这是个我真可以 lucky、有创意、在对的位置的地方，vs 感觉哦有个我知道的终态我只是得 work 到那。每当我在那个只有一种结果、我只是得到那的区域，我不是最好的我。我带不来创意、运气、兴奋同样方式。

turns.zh: 让我告诉你一个叫 Sidebar 的产品。提升职业最好的方式是 surround 自己与非凡的 peer。这给你不止一个 leg up，给你一个 leap forward。这对我在职业里非常 work，这是 Sidebar 的 ethos。当你有一群信任的 peer，你可以讨论挑战、得到职业建议、就 gut check 你怎么想工作、职业、生活。这对我是个轨迹改变者，但建这种信任 peer 群很难。(00:05:34)：Sidebar 是一个私密的、高 vetting 的领导力 program，资深 leader 被匹配到 peer 组以 lean on 无偏见意见、多元视角和 raw feedback。在 world-class program 和 facilitation 引导下，Sidebar 让你在职业旅程每一步获得聚焦、战术 feedback。如果你是这播客听众，你已 committed to 成长。Sidebar 是催化你职业的缺失那块。93% 成员说 Sidebar 帮他们在职业里实现显著正向变化。为什么花十年找你的人当你今天能在 Sidebar 遇到他们？加入数千名来自微软、亚马逊、Meta 等公司的顶级资深 leader，访问 sidebar.com/lenny。就是 sidebar.com/lenny。(00:06:26)：本期节目也由 Anvil 赞助。他们的 document SDK 帮产品团队快速 build 和上线文档软件。Carta 和 Vouch Insurance 等公司用 Anvil 加速文档工作流开发。快速上市是产品团队首要优先，你和开发者最不想的就是从零建文档工作流。耗时、贵、分心。你可以 stitch 多个工具和管理那些集成，或用 all-in-one document SDK。(00:07:00)：大多数 PM 会说……

turns.speaker: Ami Vora
turns.en: I mean, I think a lot of us are just like, you have a spreadsheet in your head of the axes and certainly when you're choosing between jobs, for me it feels like, oh man, the rest of my career hangs in the balance of making the exact right decision and getting the exact right job. And you work through all of this spreadsheet mass of, if I took this job, here's what it would do for me, here's where I'd be in five years, etc. And I have that engine in my head also, but what I try to do is work through the spreadsheets and then tear it up because none of that stuff is actually going to determine how good I am at the job. The thing that'll determine... In my track record, the thing that has determined it is when I walk through the doors, do I feel like I'm lucky to be there? (00:09:03): So for me, it's actually a lot more emotional. I try to just put on the coat of the job. When I wake up in the morning, I'm like, what would it be like if I were doing this job? What would I think about on my commute? Who would I have lunch with? Do I like them? What problems am I going to solve today? And that gives me an emotional response, which is just much more telling than the spreadsheets of, here's where I'm going to be in five years. (00:09:31): And for me, the thing that has led me to the places where I do my best work is a feeling of being at home, which is all about trust and trust with the people around me. Can I walk through and feel like these people are going to have my back, they're going to let me take risks, I'm going to enjoy spending time with them? And that's where I feel like I've always just been able to try more things and do better because a big, trust is a big unlock for me.
turns.zh: 嗯，我觉得我们很多人就脑里有轴的 spreadsheet，当然选工作时对我来说感觉像哦天哪我整个职业取决于做完全对的决定、得到完全对的工作。你过所有这个 spreadsheet 大量如果我接这个工作这是它为我做的、五年后我在哪等等。我脑里也有那个引擎，但我试图做的是过 spreadsheet 然后撕掉因为它都不决定我做这份工作多好。决定的……我的 track record 里决定的是我走过门时我感觉 lucky 在那里吗？(00:09:03)：所以对我来说其实更情感。我试穿上工作的外衣。早上醒来我想如果我在做这份工作会怎样？通勤想什么？和谁午餐？我喜欢他们吗？今天解决什么问题？那给我情感回应，比五年后我在哪的 spreadsheet 告诉我得多。(00:09:31)：对我来说，带我去我做最好工作的地方的是家的感觉，全是信任和和周围人的信任。我能走过感觉这些人会 back 我、让我 take risk、我会享受和他们待？那是我觉得我总能试更多、做更好因为信任是大 unlock 对我。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this metaphor of putting on the coat of the job, of just feeling out what it would be to work there. I imagine that was something that you did before you joined Faire, which I want to talk about, but let me transition a bit to talking about Meta and specifically, Boz. The CTO of Meta was on this podcast a few months ago and he said something about you that I want to read.
turns.zh: 我爱这个穿上工作外衣的 metaphor，就感受在那里工作怎样。我猜你加入 Faire 前做了这个，我想聊，但让我转到聊 Meta 尤其是 Boz。Meta CTO 几个月前上过这播客，他说了你一些事我想读。

turns.speaker: Ami Vora
turns.en: Oh, kind.
turns.zh: 哦，好心。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so you've heard what he said about you?
turns.zh: 好，你听过他说你什么？

turns.speaker: Ami Vora
turns.en: [inaudible 00:10:21].

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, cool. So let me read this and then I want to learn from you how to do this. So here's what he said. "Working with Ami, it was like watching an alien because she could have the most profound disagreement in the world with somebody and they would say something that she thought was not just wrong, but crazy wrong, and she would respond, 'Fascinating, you have to tell me more why you think that.' And she meant it from the core of her being. She saw this schism and rather than reacting as if it was a threat, she reacted with the most genuine and profound curiosity. I just watched it absolutely tear down walls between points of view. Embracing curiosity in those moments of challenges completely changed my life and I owe that to Ami Vora."
turns.zh: 好，酷。那我读这个然后我想跟你学怎么做。这是他说的：「和 Ami 工作像看外星人因为她可以和人有最深的分歧、他们说一些她觉得不只错、是疯狂错的事，她会回应『有趣，你得告诉我更多你为什么那么想。』她从核心真心这么说。她看到这个 schism，而非 react 像是威胁，她以最真诚和最深刻的好奇 react。我就看它绝对拆掉观点之间的墙。在挑战时刻拥抱好奇心完全改变了我的人生，我欠 Ami Vora 这个。」

turns.speaker: Ami Vora
turns.en: Oh man, I love Boz, what a great guy, and so kind of him to say that. I mean, I will say that this did not come naturally to me. I really enjoy being right, I love to be right. I think most of us love being right, and at least in my childhood, part of my identity was built on being the person who was right and being the person who knew everything. (00:11:22): And then it turns out that in the working world, that did not serve me so great, it wasn't great to walk into things and be like, all y'all are wrong, I am the only answer, everyone please to listen to me and stop talking. And what really happened was that someone pointed out to me that not only... One of my old managers pointed out to me that not only was I spending a lot of energy trying to think through every possible thing by myself so I could be totally right, I was often not really coming to the right answer. Other people have a bunch of information that I do not have. And so I'm just ignoring that, I was letting my ego overtake my desire to get to the best outcome, which is just, that's a silly trade off and an unnecessary one. (00:12:12): The thing that changed there is me just saying it's more important for us to get to the outcome and I very selfishly just like to learn more things. And so by deciding that I already knew everything, I was cutting myself off from learning the things that other people were really good at and it's so easy to just open the door instead and say like, hey, you seem to know something that I don't know yet. Why not tell me about it? I'm going to get better. We'll probably come to the right outcome. Maybe you'll have a better time. Why not? (00:12:45): And so it was a little bit just accidental evolution in that direction. But it's made work and life so much more interesting to just be like, hey, what does this person know that I don't know yet? It means that every meeting you walk into, you're probably not going to get bored and I get bored a lot, but if you assume that every person there knows something that you don't know, then it's not just wait to get to the right answer, it's like, discover the thing that they know that you don't know and it becomes just a little bit of uncovering.
turns.zh: 天哪，我爱 Boz，多好的人，他那么好心说那个。嗯，我会说这个对我不自然。我很享受 being right、我爱对。我觉得我们大多爱对，至少我童年部分身份建在是那个对的人、知道一切的人身上。(00:11:22)：然后 turns out 在工作世界那对我没那么好用，走进去就「你们都错，我是唯一答案，大家请听我、停止说话」不好。真正发生的是有人指出我，我一个老 manager 指出我不只花很多能量自己想每件可能的事以便 totally 对，我经常其实没到对答案。别人有一堆我没有的信息。我在 ignore 那个、让 ego 接管我对最好结果的渴望，那是 silly 权衡和不必要的。(00:12:12)：改变的是我说到达结果更重要，我非常 selfish 地想学更多东西。所以决定我已知道一切我在切断自己从学别人很擅长的事，开门说嘿你似乎知道我还不知道的。为什么不告诉我？我会变好。我们大概到对结果。也许你会更开心。为什么不？(00:12:45)：所以有点意外朝那个方向进化。但它让工作和生活有趣得多，就嘿这个人知道什么我还不知道？意味着你走进每个会议大概不会无聊，我经常无聊，但如果你假设每个……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: For people that want to learn to be good at this the way you are, a couple things that I take away from the historian and the way you're talking about this is, one is there's an enthusiasm of, I disagree with you, but I want you to know I really care about what you think. So there's an energy of like, please tell me what I'm missing. There's also this assumption that a lot of disagreement is rooted in, we just have different information, so tell me what I'm missing. Can you talk a bit about just how to, what you've learned about actually do this well?
turns.zh: 想学像你这样擅长这个的人，我从 historian 和你聊这个 take away 几件事：一是有热情「我不同意你但我想让你知道我真在乎你怎么想」。有能量 like 请告诉我我 miss 什么。还有这个假设很多分歧根在我们就是有不同信息，所以告诉我我 miss 什么。能聊聊你学到怎么实际做好这个？

turns.speaker: Ami Vora
turns.en: Yeah, I mean, I think the hard part is just sublimating your ego a little bit and saying it's more important to get to the outcome than to be right. And I think all of growth is a battle with yourself, but this is one of the hardest ones because we all want to be right, we all want to protect ourselves and it served us, many of us for so long to be right. I just try to think about the feedback loop of, I think all of life is feedback loops, so I just started to think about the feedback loop I'm creating of like, I was curious about something. I learned something new, we got for a better outcome. Probably the other person felt better as well as I felt better. It's all positive feedback and you do that a couple of times and the positive feedback far outweighs the desire to be right because now we're more right, we're more right together. And so just building that as a practice of just noticing how much better things can get when you can be open to them, has been really fun.
turns.zh: 对，我觉得难的是 sublimating 你的 ego 一点，说到达结果比 being right 更重要。所有成长是和自己战斗，这是最难的之一因为我们都要对、都要保护自己、它 serve 了我们很多人很久。我就想 feedback loop，我觉得所有生活是 feedback loop，所以我开始想我创建的 feedback loop：我对什么好奇、学了新东西、得到更好结果。大概对方也感觉更好、我也感觉更好。全是正反馈，你做几次正反馈远超过 being right 的欲望因为现在我们更对、一起更对。所以把它作为 practice 注意事可以变多好当你 open，真的有趣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What do you think of this phrase that he used that he remembers? Is that a phrase that you find useful? Just fascinating, you have to tell me more why you think that.
turns.zh: 你觉得他记得的他用的那个短语有用吗？就「有趣，你得告诉我更多你为什么那么想。」

turns.speaker: Ami Vora
turns.en: I do think that is a word that I say a lot. I do say that a lot, because it's true, it's fascinating that someone to look at the same movie that I was looking at and come away with a totally different understanding of the plot. I could sit in the same meeting as other people and they would leave with just a different retelling of what happened, and that to me is fascinating. Isn't that surprising, that we can all see the same, what we think are the same facts and walk away with a totally different narrative? And when you really go deep into that and you just understand how people see the world, and that is helpful. I'm curious about things, I like to know more things, and so that just helps me know more things.
turns.zh: 我确实说那个词很多。我说那个很多，因为是真的，有趣有人看和我一样的电影得出完全不同理解。我可以坐在同一个会议别人离开就不同复述发生了什么，那对我来说有趣。不是 surprising 吗，我们看同样的、我们以为是同样事实走出完全不同 narrative？当你真深入那个、理解人怎么看世界，那有帮助。我对东西好奇、想知道更多，那帮我知更多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like the hardest part of this for people is you hear someone say something, say, okay, so our mutual friend, Dan Hockenmaier, he's in a meeting and he just says something that you are just like, no, because he's got influence. He's a big deal at Faire. Most people have this visceral reaction of like, oh no, I really don't think that's a good idea. Is there something you've learned about controlling that bodily reaction of like, oh, and then just being positive about it?
turns.zh: 我觉得对人来说最难的是你听人说什么，比如我们共同朋友 Dan Hockenmaire 他在会议里就说一些你就「不」因为他有影响。他在 Faire 大 deal。大多人有这个身体反应像「哦不，我真不觉得那好 idea」。你学到控制那个身体反应「哦」然后 positive 对它吗？

turns.speaker: Ami Vora
turns.en: Yeah, I do think it is just that feedback loop. It's not like I don't have the visceral reaction, it's just that instead of interpreting it as this is a visceral reaction, I got to shut something down, it's like, this is a visceral reaction and it's a chance to learn more. Just reinterpreting some of the feelings in ways that are more about opening than about closing stuff down.
turns.zh: 对，我觉得就是那个 feedback loop。不是我没身体反应，就是而不是解释成这是身体反应我得 shut 什么下，是这是身体反应、是学更多的机会。就 reinterpret 一些感受成更关于 opening 而非 closing。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it, so it's kind of like a thinking you do of like, okay, hey, let me frame this and think about this [inaudible 00:16:28].
turns.zh: 懂，所以有点像你做的思考 like 好让我 frame 这个、想这个。

turns.speaker: Ami Vora
turns.en: For me the most important thing is just taking a pause. I think when you just take a pause, your body calms down, your mind gets a chance to breathe a little bit, and then your response is going to be better, but you got to take the pause because the immediate visceral reaction, is not always... It's going to be primal, it's going to be protective. It's just when you take a pause you're like, this is all fine, let's just learn.
turns.zh: 对我来说最重要的是暂停一下。你暂停一下身体平静、脑子有机会呼吸、然后回应更好，但你得暂停因为即时身体反应不总……会是 primal、protective。当你暂停就「都 fine，让我们学。」

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like more people are going to start using this phrase, fascinating.
turns.zh: 我觉得更多人会开始用这个词：有趣。

turns.speaker: Ami Vora
turns.en: Fascinating.
turns.zh: 有趣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: When they hear something [inaudible 00:16:58].
turns.zh: 当他们听到什么[听不清]。

turns.speaker: Ami Vora
turns.en: It's kind of my tagline. There were a few years where I had to be careful about not saying it because whenever I said it, people would be like, she disagrees. So I've had to use a thesaurus and expand my words I use.
turns.zh: 有点我的 tagline。有几年我得小心不说它因为每当我说大家就「她不同意」。所以我得用 thesaurus 扩展我用的词。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No, that's such a good word. Maybe we'll make that the title of this episode.
turns.zh: 不，那是个好词。也许我们让那个成为这期 title。

turns.speaker: Ami Vora
turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 完全。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What a great title that would be. So we've been talking a bit about the bodily reaction to stuff and our lizard brain almost, reacting to things. It reminds me of this metaphor that you called the dinosaur brain and how it applies to product reviews. Talk about what that is.
turns.zh: 多好的 title。我们聊了一点身体反应和蜥蜴脑对东西 react。让我想到你叫恐龙脑的 metaphor 和它怎么 apply 到产品 review。聊那个。

turns.speaker: Ami Vora
turns.en: Okay, so a lot of people on my team, they're coming in to do product reviews and they're worried about it. They're stressed out, they don't exactly know what to show, and the normal temptation is just to show as much information as possible because that way you come in and you think, hey, the people in this room are super smart. I'll show them the information, they will come to the right conclusions. They'll probably make a better decision than I'm going to make. So my job is to catalog the information and present it. (00:17:59): And one of the first things that I talk to people about is, okay, for the purposes of this conversation, I'm going to put myself in the capitally executive bucket because that makes what I'm about to say less offensive. Assume that executives have a little tiny dinosaur brain. We all have a little brontosaurus brain and we can really only hold three facts at the same time. We will never be able to go deep in the way that you are able to do on everything that crosses our desk. And so the best service you can do is actually do the work of making a recommendation. That's the way we're going to be complimentary. The breadth that I normally have to look across means that I'm going to be better at things like pattern matching or giving you more context or telling you stuff that's happening in the company or the industry. But what I'm not going to be better at is looking at all the information that you looked at and coming up with a meaningful outcome. That's what you're going to do and my little dinosaur brain is going to be like, okay, that sounds like a very reasonable pattern, I've seen other patterns that look like this. Okay, that sounds like an outcome, however, it conflicts with this outcome over here. I can tell you about that. Does that make sense?
turns.zh: 好，我团队很多人来做产品 review、担心、压力、不确切知道 show 什么，正常诱惑是 show 尽可能多信息因为那样你进来想嘿这个房间的人超聪明。我 show 信息他们会到对结论。大概会做比我更好的决策。所以我是 catalog 信息和呈现。(00:17:59)：我和大家聊的第一件事是好，为这个对话目的我把自己放进高管桶因为那让我要说的不那么 offensive。假设高管有小小的恐龙脑。我们都有小雷龙脑同时只能 hold 三个事实。我们永远没法像你在每个过我们桌的东西上深入。所以你能做的最好服务是真的做工作做推荐。那是我们互补的方式。我通常看的广度意味着我更擅长 pattern matching 或给你更多 context 或告诉你公司或行业发生什么。但我不擅长的是看你看的所有信息得出 meaningful 结果。那是你做的、我小恐龙脑就「好，听起来合理 pattern，我见过其他 pattern 像这样。好，听起来结果，但它和那边结果冲突。我能告诉你那个。」make sense 吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, and I love that you put yourself in that bucket. You have a dinosaur brain also, it's not other people.
turns.zh: 对，我爱你把自己放那个桶。你也有恐龙脑，不是别人。

turns.speaker: Ami Vora
turns.en: It's a pretty bad, bad look, but it's really true. As you get more breadth, you are less and less able to go deep on everything that deserves going deep and you just end up doing a different service than the people on your team, and recognizing that as complimentary has been really helpful.
turns.zh: 挺 bad look 但真的。你广度越广越没法在每个该深入的深入，你做和团队不同的服务，认识那个互补很有帮助。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You have this phrase, my manager owns context, I own the recommendation. Kind of along the same lines?
turns.zh: 你有这句话：我的 manager 拥有 context，我拥有推荐。差不多同一线？

turns.speaker: Ami Vora
turns.en: Exactly, very similar. And I think the thing that was helpful for me there is that really unlocked what I was looking for from my managers because otherwise I wanted them to be exactly like me. If I assume that I need to bring them information and then they would come to the same conclusion that I would come to, that's very narrow. They have to be able to look at the exact same information and process it in the same way and come out with the same idea. Whereas if what they're doing is complimentary to me, then I can learn from everyone. They're going to just have a different view, they're going to have new information that I don't have, and it gives me a lot more space to take accountability.
turns.zh: exactly，非常类似。我觉得对我有帮助的是那 unlock 了我在 manager 找什么因为否则我想要他们和我一样。如果我假设我需要带信息他们会到同样结论，那很窄。他们得能看同样信息、同样处理、出同样 idea。而如果他们做的是互补我就能从每个人学。他们会有不同 view、新信息我没有，给我更多空间 take accountability。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there any other advice that you could share along these lines of just product reviews? So, the big takeaway here is just keep it simple and have a recommendation.
turns.zh: 还有什么建议你能分享这条线就产品 review？大 takeaway 就是保持简单、有推荐。

turns.speaker: Ami Vora
turns.en: Keep it simple, have a recommendation. I also think that, I think we misuse product reviews sometimes as ways to get decisions and actually, they should be ways to calibrate on principles. So what you don't want is to come to a product review for every single that you want to make. Instead, what you want is to come to a product review with one decision, but the goal of that decision is to walk out with principles about how to make these decisions in the future so that you don't have to come to product review, but you still have this consistent and coherent product that you're building. (00:21:04): And so I think when you flip the frame of reviews to being less about, okay, I'm going to bring this information to an exec, my manager, whoever, and they're going to decide every piece, you're not actually building that much more capacity in the system. You're getting fast decision making, but you're not changing who can make really good decisions. And I think you always want to change the org to constantly make better decisions, and a way to do that is when you bring these sorts of questions, what you talk about is, why did you make this decision? What are the trade-offs you have in mind? Who are you optimizing for? What timeline are you thinking about? What's the risk level we're willing to tolerate? And then you don't have to come back. You have enough information that you can take those principles and run with them.
turns.zh: 保持简单、有推荐。我也觉得我们有时误用产品 review 作为获取决策的方式，其实该是校准原则的方式。你不想要每个小决策都来产品 review。而是你带一个决策来产品 review，但那个决策的目的是带着关于未来怎么决策的原则走出去，这样你不必来产品 review 但仍有连贯一致的产品。(00:21:04)：当你 flip review 的 frame 从「我带信息给 exec、manager、谁、他们决定每块」到那个，你其实没建多少更多 capacity 在系统里。你得到快决策但没改变谁能做真好决策。我觉得你总想改组织不断做更好决策，一个方式是当你带这种问题时你谈的是为什么你做这个决策？你有什么 trade-off？你 optimize 给谁？你想什么时间线？我们愿意容忍什么风险？然后你不必回来。你有足够信息可以拿那些原则跑。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a framework or a process you use for product reviews that might be helpful for people to hear? Just like a agenda or a way of thinking about just how to set up a product review for success? Because a lot of people are trying to set these up at their companies and they're like, I don't know if we're doing this optimally.
turns.zh: 有没有你用的 framework 或流程可能对大家有帮助？就像 agenda 或怎么 set 产品 review 成功？因为很多人在公司 set 这些就「我不知道我们做得最优吗。」

turns.speaker: Ami Vora
turns.en: Yeah, I think everyone's got... I think there's so many different takes on frameworks. I don't have a single system. I mean, actually I think Boz has written about a bunch of this, and I probably most agree with him. Where there's different kinds of product reviews, it's like, what are you trying to solve? What's the timeline on which you're thinking about for these? Is it a philosophy? Is it a strategic shift? Is it a day-to-day product decision? And then keeping it extremely short and pointed and then making sure you walk away with principles, not answers.
turns.zh: 对，我觉得大家有……有很多不同 framework take。我没单一系统。其实我觉得 Boz 写过一堆，我大概最同意他。有不同种产品 review，是你在解决什么？你想什么时间线？是哲学？是战略转变？是日常产品决策？然后保持极短、pointed、然后确保带走原则不是答案。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think there's a lot of nuance and importance there of what you just said, which is start with the problem you're solving. What are we trying to do here? And the timeline, I think that's also really useful and important for people to hear.
turns.zh: 我觉得你刚说的有很多 nuance 和重要：从你解决的问题开始。我们在做什么？时间线我觉得也很有用重要。

turns.speaker: Ami Vora
turns.en: I think the temptation is always to err toward writing more, and what I always really recommend people do is write whatever you need to write and then cut out almost all of it. What you really want to bring to any forum, whether it's a product review or a written inform or anything else, is the minimal amount of information that you need to make a clean recommendation because then you are forced to be opinionated. Otherwise, the opinion can get lost in all of this information. You can hide behind, well, all of these analyses seem to suggest, and instead you should probably just say, looked at all the data, there's three analyses that suggest this. There's one that suggests that, we think that one is inaccurate or worth taking the risk on. Let's go. Any objections? Let me know. Any new context? Let me know. That really forces you to deeply understand and take an opinion on the material.
turns.zh: 我觉得诱惑总是写更多，我总推荐写你需要写的然后 cut 掉几乎全部。你真想带到任何 forum——产品 review 或 written inform 或别的——是最少信息你需要做清晰推荐因为那样你被迫 opinionated。否则 opinion 会在所有信息里丢。你可以 hide 在「嗯所有这些分析似乎 suggest」背后，而你应该说看了所有数据、三个分析 suggest 这个、一个 suggest 那个、我们觉得那个不准或值得 take risk。走。有异议？告诉我。有新 context？告诉我。那真逼你深入理解、对材料 take opinion。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Final question, who do you like to invite to these product reviews and your thoughts, rules, policy?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题，你喜欢请谁进这些产品 review？你的想法、规则、policy？

turns.speaker: Ami Vora
turns.en: Yeah, I mean I do think that usually fewer people is better. It leads to a sense of being informal and that is really useful because it lowers the bar on how complete or strong these conversations are and I'd rather have a less formal conversation faster than a formal conversation and lose three weeks in the process when we could have been building. I think it needs to be cross-functional. I think one of the things you want is cross-functional accountability. So we want it cross-functional at the leadership level and cross-functional at the team presenting level. And I think those are normally the groups. (00:24:25): I think the thing that gets hard is you often cut out the middle, where if it's a working team presenting to the senior leaders on something important, it's really hard because it means people's managers are not in the room and can't help the conversation or other things. And so in order to do that, you have to really have a bunch of implicit trust inside the team that everyone will get the context later, that everyone's going to be kind to everyone else and you don't need a ton of air cover, and that the managers trust their team to present in the best possible way.
turns.zh: 对，我觉得通常人少更好。导致 informal 感那很有用因为它降低这些对话多完整或多强的 bar，我宁愿更快有 less formal 对话 vs formal 对话在过程中丢三周当我们本可以 build。我觉得需要跨职能。你要跨职能 accountability。所以我们要领导层跨职能和呈现团队跨职能。那些通常是组。(00:24:25)：我觉得难的是你经常 cut 掉中间，如果工作团队向 senior leader 呈现重要的，很难因为人的 manager 不在房间、不能帮对话。所以要做到那个你真得有团队内一堆 implicit trust 每个人 later 得 context、每个人对每个人好、你不需要大量 air cover、manager 信任团队以最好方式呈现。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is always a stressful place for a manager to be, where their success is riding in that meeting and they're not there and they-
turns.zh: 那总是 manager 压力大的地方，成功在那个会议而他们不在、他们——

turns.speaker: Ami Vora
turns.en: It's so stressful, it's so stressful. I think anything you do to make it less stressful is useful. But then there've also been times in my career where I would keep the room itself small, but because we were all trying to calibrate on specific principles, I would record or broadcast the reading to anyone who wanted to see it, just so they could all see the principles by which we were decision-making and get calibrated on that.
turns.zh: 那么压力，那么压力。任何你做的减压力有用。但我职业里也有时我保持房间本身小，但因为我们都在校准特定原则，我会录或 broadcast reading 给任何想看的人，就让他们能看到我们做决策的原则、校准那个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So through your career you've transitioned from being the person pitching the products and being reviewed to the person reviewing and being on the other side. Is there anything being on this side of it that you think is helpful for people earlier in their career to know about that experience, from your angle now?
turns.zh: 你职业里你从 pitch 产品和被 review 的人转到 review 和另一边。从那边有什么对更早期的人有帮助知道的、你现在的角度？

turns.speaker: Ami Vora
turns.en: I mean, I think for what it's worth, I think I still do a fair amount of product pitching in the past few years because there's always someone else to convince.
turns.zh: 嗯，我觉得值多少，我觉得我过去几年仍做不少产品 pitch 因为总有别人要 convince。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's true.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Ami Vora
turns.en: Especially if you want to do something dramatically different. Really, I think the biggest service for people who are starting out a little earlier is that point around bringing the recommendation, really having the opinion and standing behind it with conviction and doing what they need to do to build that conviction for themselves.
turns.zh: 尤其你想做 dramatic 不同的。真我觉得对更早期的人最大服务是那个：带推荐、真有 opinion、用 conviction 站背后、做他们需要做的为自己建那个 conviction。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. You've done this a number of times already in this conversation, and so I want to spend a little time here, which is using metaphors and imagery to make your point and get people to understand what you're trying to say. So you have this code of putting on the coat of the job and this dinosaur brain, and so someone told me that this is just a skill you have where you use metaphor and imagery to rally a team, get your point across, get people to understand what you're trying to say. There's also this metaphor, someone told me I need to ask you about the hill climb metaphor. Does that ring a bell?
turns.zh: 太好了。你已经在这个对话里做了好几次，所以我想花点时间，就是用 metaphor 和意象传达观点、让人理解你试图说的。你有穿上工作外衣和恐龙脑，有人告诉我这是你的技能——你用 metaphor 和意象 rally 团队、传达观点、让人理解。还有这个 metaphor，有人告诉我我得问你爬山 metaphor。ring a bell 吗？

turns.speaker: Ami Vora
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, what is that all about?
turns.zh: 好，关于什么？

turns.speaker: Ami Vora
turns.en: For me, the hill climb is all about the difference between the local optimum and a global optimum. That sounds very abstract, but I think a lot of the time when we're doing our job, when we're doing life stuff, whatever you're doing, you try to just get better and better and you optimize your current system and then you feel really good about it, and that is great. You're standing on top of the hill, you're looking down, you can see the, I don't know, rolling hills, the sheep, the grass, whatever. But then way off from the distance you can see a mountain, one that's even higher than you can't even see the top of it, and you have to decide, are you going to take the risk of climbing down your hill, crossing an unknown chasm, and then climbing back up, just to get to the same level you started at with more climbing to do to get to that summit? And that is really hard. (00:27:51): I'm thinking of things like, maybe the first time I saw this was like a lot of companies were really good at desktop and you could see the mobile mountain way out over there, but to get there you had to really make a lot of trade-offs in your core desktop business that you were not totally sure were going to pay off when you made it to the mobile mountain, and you had to do a ton of work. You had to fundamentally rewire a lot of what you're doing without a guarantee that you're going to get there. I mean, you can see it in life when you think about new jobs or new moves or new relationships, anything that you think about. You are giving up something that is working pretty well without knowing whether you're going to make it to the top of that next mountain. And that's been really helpful to me just to place where I am on different things, where you get the inkling that there is a much better way to do this, there really is. (00:28:48): Is it going to be worth going down into the valley, climbing up, keeping climbing? Is that going to be worth it? Most of the time the answer is yes, but it's helpful for me to know, boy, this feels like a slog. It is supposed to? Because I'm still in the valley and the thing that gets me through the valley is remembering what the summit feels like. When you're on top of it and you're like, this is great, it was absolutely worth it. My life is better in these ways, we're able to solve these problems in these ways. It was worth it.
turns.zh: 对我来说爬山是 local optimum 和 global optimum 的区别。听起来很抽象，但我觉得我们做工作、做生活事什么的时候，你试变得更好更好、optimize 当前系统然后感觉很好，那很好。你站山顶往下看，能看到不知道 rolling hills、羊、草什么的。但远处你能看到一座山、比你甚至看不到顶的更高，你得决定你要不要冒险爬下你的山、穿过未知 chasm、然后爬回，就到同样水平你开始的加上更多爬到那个 summit？那很难。(00:27:51)：我想事比如也许第一次我看到这个是很多公司很擅长桌面、你能看到移动的山在那边，但要到那你真得在核心桌面业务做很多 trade-off 你不完全确定到了移动山会 pay off，你得做大量工作。你得从根本上 rewire 很多你在做的没有保证你会到。你能在生活里看到新工作或新移动或新关系任何你想的。你在放弃 work 得挺好的东西不知道是否会到那个下一个山顶。那对我在不同事上 place 我在哪很有帮助，你 inkling 有更好方式做这个，真有。(00:28:48)：值得下到山谷、爬上、继续爬吗？那值得吗？大多时候答案是是，但 h……

turns.en: On this kind of broader idea of metaphors and imagery, is there something there that you've learned of just like, this works really well, I'm going to invest in becoming better at this, or is this something that's come natural to you? Anything you can share about that skill and approach?

turns.speaker: Ami Vora
turns.en: I think this one came from, I worked for a manager, his name was Eric Antino, and he was just a master of the metaphor and analogies. And so whenever I would bring him something, he would be like, how is this product going to make you feel, and when is the last time that you felt this way? And you can say, oh, I felt this way when I was hanging with my friends in Dolores Park and he'd be like, cool, tell me what it feels like, why that's the analogy, what ramifications come out of that? (00:30:18): And one thing I like to do is try to build an emulator for different people in my head, because I've just had the good fortune of working with an amazing number of very different leaders, and so he's one of the people I tried to build an emulator for where I'd be like, okay, I see this thing. I don't know how to solve this problem. How would Eric describe this? I've tried to build one for Boz, which is all about principle of decision making and principle of trade-offs. There's a few other people where I'm like, I don't know how to solve this problem. Can I load this other person into my head and how would they approach it? And that gives me a fresh lens on it. (00:30:55): And I really like metaphors and analogies because I think especially as you scale a team, narrative becomes increasingly important. Narrative can carry so much weight and water where otherwise it's similar to the product review point, where either you can tell everybody exactly what to do at every point or you can create a story that we all agree on. And when we all agree on that story, people just know better what to do. If we all agree that the feeling of something should be, I'm sitting in Dolores Park with my friends on a sunny Saturday. You know what the iconography, the designers know what iconography should look like. You know what the communication and join pattern should look like. You're not going to build something cold and corporate, you're not going to build something strobe light, you're not going to build something flashy, but you don't have to go and make all those individual decisions. You can buy into the same story and then people will just naturally build something that feels more consistent.
turns.zh: 我觉得这个来自我为一个 manager 工作，他叫 Eric Antino，他是 metaphor 和 analogy 大师。所以每当带他东西他会像这产品让你感受什么、你上次什么时候感受这样？你能说哦我和朋友在 Dolores Park 感受这样，他说好告诉我感觉什么、为什么那个 analogy、什么 ramification 出来？(00:30:18)：我喜欢做的一件事是 try 为不同人在脑里建 emulator，因为我有幸和很多非常不同 leader 工作，他是其中一个我试建 emulator 的，我就好我看到这个、我不知道怎么解决、Eric 会怎么描述？我试为 Boz 建一个，全是决策原则和 trade-off 原则。还有几个别人我就好我不知道怎么解决这个。能把另一个人加载进脑里他们会怎么 approach？那给我 fresh lens。(00:30:55)：我很喜欢 metaphor 和 analogy 因为我觉得尤其 scale 团队时 narrative 越来越重要。Narrative 能 carry 很多重量和水，否则就像产品 review 那点：要么你告诉每个人每点该做什么、要么你创造一个我们都同意的故事。当我们都同意那个故事，大家就知做什么更好。如果我们都同意那个东西感觉应该是我在 Dolores Park 和朋友阳光周六。你知道 iconography、设计师知道 iconography 该长什么样。你知道沟通和 join pattern 该长什么样。你不会建冷的企业、你不会建 strobe light、你不……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is such a powerful and important skill. Is there an example that comes to mind where you did this really well, say at WhatsApp or Facebook of the story that carried a lot of water for you and the team?
turns.zh: 这么 powerful 重要技能。有例子你做得很好的 say WhatsApp 或 Facebook 的故事 carry 了很多重量？

turns.speaker: Ami Vora
turns.en: Yeah, I mean I think the product metaphor we arrived at for WhatsApp was face-to-face communication. Our goal there was to make it so that every person in the world could feel connected to the people they cared most about, even when they were separate, even they're distant geographically for whatever reason, we were always going to be apart from the people you cared about. And we really had to build something that would work for literally everyone in the world. People who are carrying these high-end devices in western markets who are very tech comfortable and savvy, and people in the low end markets who were carrying these low end devices, they weren't that familiar with technology, it was maybe their first time online. We had to build something that worked for everyone. (00:32:57): And the most universal form of communication is face-to-face. When you talk to someone face-to-face, you're not thinking, how do I present? What tool do I have to learn? You just open your mouth and words come out, and that's the feeling that we wanted to create. And that involved a lot of the app stepping back from communication, creating spaces that felt really intimate so people wouldn't have to think to themselves, what kind of space am I in? They could immediately map where they were in the app to the, okay, I'm sitting around in my kitchen table and people are joining and leaving calls just like they're walking in and out of my living room, but it is a family space and the family is there. Or, in one-on-one disappearing messages, you're like, cool, this is my close friend. We don't need to keep track of everything that we're saying. We're here for a little bit of banter, a little bit of relationship, a little bit of quick, what's your wifi password and stuff, and whatever's really important, that's what we'll hold onto and the rest is just day-to-day, normal intimacy.
turns.zh: 对，我觉得我们为 WhatsApp 到达的产品 metaphor 是面对面沟通。我们目标是让世界每个人感觉连接到他们最在乎的人，即使分开、即使地理远或什么原因，你总会和你关心的人分开。我们真得 build 适合世界每个人的东西。西方市场拿高端设备、技术舒适 savvy 的人，和低端市场拿低端设备、不太熟技术、可能第一次上网的人。我们得 build 适合每个人的。(00:32:57)：最 universal 的沟通形式是面对面。你和人面对面时你不想我该怎么 present、我得学什么工具。你就张嘴说话出来，那是我们要创造的感觉。那涉及很多 app 从沟通 step back、创造感觉 intimate 的空间让人不必想我在什么空间？他们能立即 map 他们在 app 哪里到 ok 我坐厨房桌、人加入离开 call 就像走进走出我客厅，但这是家庭空间、家庭在。或一对一消失消息你 like 好这是我的密友。我们不必 track 说的每件事。我们在这为一点 banter、一点关系、一点快速你的 wifi 密码什么，什么真重要我们 hold 住、其他就是日常正常亲密。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is super interesting. WhatsApp, one of the main differentiators and benefits is it's super fast. And I see completely how it connects this idea of you're just like, ideas, we want you to feel like you're talking to someone.
turns.zh: 那超有趣。WhatsApp 主要差异化和好处之一是超快。我完全看到它怎么连这个 idea 你就 like 想法、我们想你感觉像和人说话。

So interesting. And then this other point you made of making this emulator of a person in your head.

No. Okay, let me go look at the dashboard. You can load up these different skillsets that people have been so generous with sharing with me.

turns.zh: 我爱这个话题就 metaphor 和故事和愿景。很多人想变更好。有没有另一个例子也许用 metaphor rally 团队、做事？

And so just creating things like joinable calls, like that feeling of people popping in and just paying attention to whoever's there and letting them leave, but the call can flow on without a super heavyweight action that everyone needs to take. I think that was another one where we were just able to agree on the feeling and then you know what to build.
turns.zh: 嗯，我觉得取 WhatsApp 一部分或我们谈视频通话。我很喜欢一个 metaphor 是坐在你家家庭室当你想怎么让 call work，你坐家庭室时你不是在 schedule、不是不知道有这种冷企业感像开 conference 那种 heavyweight 互动，而是你可以加入和离开。感觉轻量、感觉空间即使你不在也存在。所以建可加入 call 那种感觉人 pop in 就注意谁在、让他们走、但 call 可以 flow on 不需要每个人 take super heavyweight action。我觉得那是另一个我们同意感觉然后你知道 build 什么。

turns.speaker: Ami Vora
turns.en: Yeah, I don't know if I coined execution eats strategy for breakfast, I think a lot of things eat other things for breakfast, but I'm a believer. I do think execution eats strategy for breakfast and that's something we used to say a lot at Meta. It was just the most important part and I was well-trained in that. That was one of the key lessons that I learned there, and it's because when you have... Look, strategy is super fun. You get to think about all this pie in the sky stuff. You get to think about if the world operated in rational patterns and you could predict the future, what is going to be the second and third order effect? You get to use your brain in a really fun, philosophical way, but customers don't care. Customers don't care about your fancy strategies and your five-year plan. They care about the product that's in their hands. And so anything that distracts you from thinking about the product in your hands I think, or maybe worse, takes you away from solving customer's problems today, I think is a distraction. (00:39:03): And I think one of the things that you learn is if you have great strategy, perfect strategy but poor execution, you don't win because your strategy never makes it to the market. And what's even worse is that you have learned nothing. You don't know whether it was your strategy that was wrong or whether it was your execution that was wrong, all you know is you didn't win. Whereas when you have a pretty good strategy, a good enough strategy, you're in the right direction and you have perfect execution, you still don't win immediately, but you know your execution was great. So then you learn, what do you need to do to improve your strategy? You've got the execution machine, you go back, you update your strategy, you relaunch, and you keep on doing it until your strategy is perfect and then you do win. And that's the lesson I repeatedly learned.
turns.zh: 对，我不知道我 coined execution eats strategy for breakfast，很多东西吃别的东西当早餐，但我信。我确实觉得执行吃战略当早餐，这是我们在 Meta 常说的。最重要部分，我在那训练有素。那是我在那学到的关键教训之一，因为当你有……看，战略超有趣。你可以想所有 pie in the sky 的东西。想如果世界理性运作、你能预测未来，二阶三阶效应是什么？你可以用脑在有趣哲学方式，但客户不在乎。客户不在乎你 fancy 战略和五年计划。他们在乎手里的产品。所以任何让你从想手里产品分心的我觉得，或更糟、让你离开今天解决客户问题，我觉得是分心。(00:39:03)：你学到的一件事是如果你有伟大战略、完美战略但执行差，你不赢因为战略从不到市场。更糟的是你什么都没学。你不知道是战略错还是执行错，你只知道你没赢。而当你有挺好战略、够好的战略、方向对、执行完美，你仍不立即赢但你知道执行很好。所以你学，你需要做什么改进战略？你有执行机器、回去、更新战略、重新 launch、继续做直到战略完美然后你赢。那是我反复学的教训。
